items.text:
Trump spent Tuesday renaming artificial intelligence “superintelligence", and putting out the fine China. Guess who's coming for dinner? 

Meta Connect opens today on the opposite coast. Somewhere a protocol officer is changing “AI” to “SI” on the place cards while Zuckerberg is deciding whether Watermelon is a fruit or a foundation model. 

The AI rumorboard is quiet, so I’m keeping the smoke short and spending time on the things that actually moved.

Alibaba’s Apsara conference keeps producing nuggets. Qwen 4 in training, not released, while conference chatter points toward a family eventually including Max, Plus, Flash and, most interestingly for the local crowd, a 27B.  The bigger Apsara story is that Alibaba is assembling the entire machine around Qwen: models, agents, chips, datacenters and now a truly enormous network fabric. AlibabaCloud Yesterday everybody understandably stared at the new Zhenwu V900 accelerator. I may have underweighted what connects those chips together.

HPN 8.0 Pro is Alibaba Cloud’s new proprietary AI network architecture, rated at 100 petabits of aggregate bandwidth. A single cluster can support more than 130,000 800G network ports, with built-in redundancy designed so optical-transceiver or link failures do not stop service. Alibaba says the new design cuts the impact of network upgrades and failures from roughly 50% to 25%. And unless the transformer architecture can be replaced with something more network efficient, that is the way forward.

Meanwhile, China has a much uglier story brewing. The Information reports that the Cyberspace Administration of China is investigating DeepSeek and Moonshot after Anthropic alleged that both companies silently routed some customer traffic through Claude and used resulting exchanges in distillation work.  Anthropic claims Moonshot routed more than 23 million exchanges during the period it studied and DeepSeek more than 12.1 million, with some traffic containing sensitive corporate, police, state and military-related data. Those are Anthropic’s allegations, not findings. 

And one actual model release got completely steamrolled by Opus, Sol, and Luna yesterday.
Tencent quietly released HY-Image 3.5 Preview.
The API does text-to-image, image-to-image and multi-turn conversational editing, can carry editing history across turns, accepts up to 20 reference images, and supports output as large as 4096×4096. International pricing is about $0.024 per 2K image, and reference images are not separately charged. Tencent claims a 30% preference improvement over HY-Image 3.0, but there is no independent leaderboard result yet and Tencent disclosed essentially nothing about the architecture. 

Aeon, the OpenAI breadcrumb, continues to make the rounds.  The original clue was a reported gpt-6-astra-aeon feature-flag string. This week reverse-engineering reports describing Aeon-specific concepts such as model choice, agent appearance, cloud environment and a dedicated thread/startAeon operation. One extracted instruction describes the system as a persistent background agent intended to maintain an ongoing understanding of the user’s goals, priorities and work. Reddit reverse-engineering found similar aeon_core_instructions. It may not be a model, but an identity layer above Codex: persistent state, ongoing cloud execution and an agent that survives individual sessions.

Important caveat: the evidence is messy. 

One independent CLI compatibility project says gpt-6-astra-aeon is not currently present as a selectable Codex binary model and warns that raw string scraping produces false model IDs. So there is something Aeon-shaped in the ecosystem, but I would not turn that into “OpenAI launches Aeon Thursday” yet. 

Which leads directly to my biggest practical OpenAI question today: what the hell is GPT-6 Sol Medium doing to Codex allowances?

On my own run, the five-hour and weekly percentages dropped much quicker when swapping GPT-6 Sol medium for 5.6 Sol Medium.  If that behavior repeats, the effective weekly burn could be several times higher than what I was accustomed to. I haven't had enough time to call it a confirmed 3x-5× multiplier. But for all of the efficiency talk, the game seems changed for the worse, again.

Reddit says I’m not staring at the gauges alone. Users were already reporting unusually aggressive Sol Medium consumption before GPT-6: one simple CRM lookup reportedly burned 8% of a five-hour allowance, while another OpenAI developer-community user said a 5.6 Sol Medium session exhausted an entire five-hour window in about 12 minutes. 

And Meta Connect starts today. The most credible AI traces are not Watermelon yet. Meta’s developer platform has unreleased Video Playground, Voice Playground and Connectors sections, which could point to Muse Video/API and broader agent integrations. “Watermelon” remains the rumored post-Avocado family, but researchers looking through Meta’s current platform code say they have not found that name there. 

The funniest confirmed Meta story is that Muse is testing a human concierge for some phone calls. We have apparently spent several trillion dollars getting autonomous agents advanced enough to rediscover the administrative assistant. Which should make the anti data center crowd happy, we have a place for you making appointments should you get the axe.

So that’s Wednesday. And Xi lands in Washington.  Zuk on the keynote, and me... token coping.

items.text:
Airdrops have always had the potential to do more than just distribute tokens, and I think @meta_alchemist is taking that idea in a much more interesting direction with @vibevibefun.

What stands out to me is the focus on making the airdrop itself part of the community-building mechanism.

The concept of “graduation airdrops” using onchain data, AI and social integrations could help projects identify the people who are actually supporting them instead of simply rewarding wallets that farm and immediately sell.

I also like the idea of bonding curves being connected with airdrops. If the distribution is structured around the growth of a project and the people contributing to it, the community becomes part of the launch rather than just an audience watching from outside.

And this goes beyond airdrops.

@vibevibefun is trying to bring together builders, products, stock pairs, RWA, memetic culture and AI-driven systems inside the launchpad. That combination could create a very different environment for projects launching on Robinhood Chain.

The part I’m most curious about is how the intelligence system will actually make those “smart picks” and determine who has genuinely contributed value.

If they can execute that properly, I can see why @meta_alchemist believes this could bring a new wave of users and builders back into crypto.

Definitely one of the parts of the ecosystem I’ll be watching closely.

$NNBR Following Q2'26 earnings, I adjusted my FY26 forecasts to revenue and EBITDA of $491M and $66M, respectively, both at or towards the high-end of mgmt's new guidance released yesterday [Revenue: $470-$490M; EBITDA: $58-$68M]. 

The rationale reflects the lower yields and margins associated with doing large ramps, which I expect to weigh on margin some. So while I believe mgmt will execute on the top-line, I anticipate there to be some modest margin impact that will be phased out as production of liquid cooling components inches towards normalized levels. But also consider the large number of new programs ramping as well in other business lines in H2'26 (defense & electronics, grid, medical, etc.).

Mgmt is presenting at the D.A. Davidson Diversified Industrial & Services, which I hope to tune in to and expect more color around the newly issued guidance. It is clear that, despite the recent market meltdown, NNBR continues to win new business and launch new programs. NNBR has begun to trade more with the AI basket of names, reasonable given its rapidly rising exposure to liquid cooling and other data center solutions.

While the fears over efforts to slow AI advancements and reduce AI investments, especially for infrastructure persist, AI is not the entire NNBR book. Mgmt has been building a manufacturing platform with a diverse book of business across, not just liquid cooling components which is a new product line, but also a robust and growing Defense & Electronics business, grid solutions, and medical. Even if investments in AI infrastructure are hit, NNBR's other target markets continue to have durable, long-term tailwinds. It's been the liquid cooling business that receives the bulk of the attention. 

The new guidance further supports the transition in my thesis from a while ago from NNBR being a turnaround play, to an overall longer-term hold due to structural advantages in its capabilities, know-how, scale, and execution and being a behind the scenes / deep in the supply chain beneficiary of substantial tailwinds across the highest growth areas.
